note: Indicative rotation read from market history — a learning tool, not fund-flow data.

countries.name: United States
countries.rule_of_law: Very strong — deep legal protection for minority shareholders
countries.demographics: Slow growth, propped up by immigration — better than most rich countries
countries.currency_note: The rupee has weakened ~3%/yr vs the dollar over decades, which ADDS to an Indian investor's dollar returns. That tailwind is the main reason US exposure has worked so well from India.
countries.access: Easy — via Indian international mutual funds/FoFs, or directly under the RBI's $250k/yr LRS window.
risks: Roughly a third of the index sits in a handful of AI/tech giants
Valuation is in its top ~2% ever — little room for error
Profit margins are at record highs and may mean-revert
tailwinds: The world's best businesses and deepest capital markets
headwinds: Near-record CAPE historically precedes weak 10-yr returns
countries.outlook: Superb businesses at a demanding price. You are paying for quality and for the AI story — expect the next decade's returns to come from earnings, not from the multiple going higher.
countries.verdict: Wonderful companies, unwonderful price. Own it for quality, not for value — and size the position knowing a de-rating would hurt.
countries.india_angle: US rate cuts push money toward India; a US sell-off drags Nifty down with it via FII outflows. The US is the tide that moves India's boat.

news.title: Gold drops 3% as Fed's Warsh comments lift rate hike bets
Wall Street Week Ahead: Jobs report, Broadcom results pose next hurdles for stock market rally
Fed’s preferred inflation gauge shows core prices rose 3.3% annually in July
Fed Chairman Warsh expresses concern about inflation, advocates for 'quieter' central bank

countries.name: Canada
countries.demographics: Growing via high immigration — a rarity in the developed world
countries.currency_note: The Canadian dollar tracks oil. A commodity slump hits both the index and the currency at once — a double blow for a foreign holder.
countries.access: Easy via global/international funds; rarely a standalone allocation.
risks: Some of the world's highest household debt and stretched housing
Banks + energy are most of the index
tailwinds: Rule of law and stable institutions
countries.outlook: A steady, dividend-rich, resource-and-banks market. Fairly priced, unlikely to shoot the lights out either way.
countries.verdict: Reasonable and boring — the kind of market you own for income, not excitement. Watch the housing debt.
countries.india_angle: A useful read on global oil/commodity demand, which flows straight into India's import bill and inflation.

news.title: India sees Canada export opening as US trade tensions reshape imports: Report

countries.name: Brazil
countries.rule_of_law: Moderate — functioning courts, but政 policy risk and corruption history
countries.demographics: Young-ish but ageing faster than expected
countries.currency_note: THE catch. The real has been a serial destroyer of foreign returns — a cheap market that keeps getting cheaper in dollar terms. High local returns have repeatedly been wiped out by the currency.
countries.access: Via EM/global funds; a direct standalone position is unusual for retail.
countries.outlook: Statistically one of the cheapest markets on earth, with high yields — and a currency that has historically taken much of that away.
countries.verdict: Cheap for a reason. The business math works; the currency and politics are what you're really underwriting. Munger would ask whether you trust the government more than the discount.
countries.india_angle: A commodity exporter — it tends to prosper when India (an importer) is squeezed by high oil and metals prices.

countries.name: Mexico
countries.rule_of_law: Moderate — improving markets, but security and policy concerns
countries.demographics: Young and growing — a real advantage
countries.currency_note: The peso is volatile but has been surprisingly resilient, supported by high interest rates and remittances.
risks: Almost entirely dependent on US demand
tailwinds: Prime nearshoring beneficiary as supply chains leave China
countries.outlook: The clearest winner from factories relocating closer to the US — priced reasonably, but a narrow, US-dependent market.
countries.verdict: A good story at a fair price, but you're really making one bet: American demand. Concentration is the hidden risk.
countries.india_angle: Competes with India for the same 'China+1' manufacturing capital.

countries.name: United Kingdom
countries.rule_of_law: Very strong — centuries of shareholder-protection law
countries.currency_note: Sterling is volatile but not a chronic decliner. Note the FTSE's earnings are largely global, so a weak pound often LIFTS the index.
countries.outlook: A cheap, high-dividend, globally-earning developed market that the world has ignored for a decade.
countries.verdict: The classic value investor's developed market: dull, unloved, cash-generative, and cheap. Returns come from dividends, not from growth.
countries.india_angle: The FTSE is commodity- and energy-heavy, so it moves with the same oil and metal prices that drive India's inflation.

countries.name: Germany
countries.demographics: Ageing and shrinking workforce — a genuine long-term drag
countries.currency_note: Euro exposure; broadly stable versus the rupee over long periods.
risks: High energy costs since losing cheap Russian gas
headwinds: China slowdown hits its exporters hardest
countries.outlook: Fairly priced world-class industrials facing real structural headwinds in energy and demographics.
countries.verdict: Good companies, difficult neighbourhood. The energy-cost problem is structural, not cyclical — that's the thing to watch.
countries.india_angle: German industrial demand pulls Indian auto-component and engineering exporters along with it.

countries.name: France
countries.demographics: Better birth rate than most of Europe, still ageing
risks: High government debt and recurring fiscal/political friction
Luxury demand heavily tied to Chinese consumers
tailwinds: Global luxury and industrial champions with real pricing power
countries.outlook: Home to some of the world's best consumer-brand moats, priced slightly above its own average.
countries.verdict: Genuinely great franchises (the luxury names have enviable pricing power) at a full-ish price. It's a back-door bet on the Chinese consumer.
countries.india_angle: Broad European risk appetite drives global EM flows, India included.

news.title: Global Markets | European shares rise as French stocks rebound; markets digest Warsh speech

countries.name: India
countries.rule_of_law: Moderate-to-good — solid company law, slow courts, improving regulator (SEBI)
countries.demographics: The world's best — a young, growing workforce for decades
countries.currency_note: Home currency — no FX risk for you. (Note the flip side: the rupee's long slide is exactly what boosts your foreign holdings.)
countries.access: Direct — this is your home market.
risks: One of the most expensive large markets in the world
Priced for years of flawless earnings delivery
Vulnerable to FII outflows when the dollar strengthens
tailwinds: Powerful domestic SIP inflows cushioning foreign selling
headwinds: Rich valuations leave no margin for error
countries.outlook: The best long-run growth story in the world, trading at a price that already assumes a lot of it comes true.
countries.verdict: Great story, high price. Growth must be delivered, not just hoped for — at this CAPE, a stumble in earnings hurts twice (lower profits AND a lower multiple).
countries.india_angle: Home. Everything else on this map is judged against what you can already get here — and the bar is high.

news.title: India sees Canada export opening as US trade tensions reshape imports: Report
Tech leads D-Street bound, FPI play in focus

countries.name: China
countries.rule_of_law: Weak for outside shareholders — the state can and does override company interests
countries.demographics: Shrinking and ageing fast — a serious structural headwind
countries.currency_note: The yuan is managed by the state — less volatile day to day, but its level is a policy decision, not a market one.
countries.access: Via EM/China funds; direct access is restricted.
risks: Policy can wipe out an industry overnight (as education did)
Ownership often via offshore structures, not real equity
tailwinds: World-leading manufacturing, EV and battery industries
countries.outlook: Genuinely cheap, genuinely troubled. The gap between its industrial strength and its stock-market performance is the puzzle.
countries.verdict: The classic value trap question: is it cheap, or is it cheap for good reason? Munger famously owned China — and equally famously, the risk here isn't the business, it's whether shareholders are allowed to keep the gains.
countries.india_angle: China stimulus lifts metals (Tata Steel, Hindalco). Global 'sell expensive India, buy cheap China' rotations are a real and recurring pressure on Nifty.

news.title: India sees Canada export opening as US trade tensions reshape imports: Report

countries.name: Japan
countries.demographics: The developed world's worst — shrinking, rapidly ageing
countries.currency_note: The yen is the big swing factor. A weak yen flatters exporters' profits but erodes what a foreign holder actually takes home.
risks: Rate normalisation could unwind global carry trades
tailwinds: A genuine corporate-governance revolution — buybacks, unwinding cross-holdings, pressure to raise returns
Still below its own long-run valuation
headwinds: Export exposure to a global slowdown
countries.outlook: A rare developed market that is NOT expensive, in the middle of the most meaningful corporate reform in its modern history.
countries.verdict: The most interesting developed market right now: improving returns on capital, cheap versus its own history, and management finally being told to care about shareholders. The debt and demographics are the price of admission.
countries.india_angle: A yen carry-trade unwind can jolt global risk appetite and pull money out of EM — including India — very fast.

countries.name: South Korea
countries.rule_of_law: Good on paper; the 'Korea discount' comes from chaebol governance that has historically shortchanged minority holders
countries.demographics: The world's lowest birth rate — a severe long-term problem
countries.currency_note: The won is highly cyclical — it falls hard in global risk-off episodes, exactly when the index is already falling.
risks: The 'Korea discount' — family-controlled conglomerates and weak minority protections
North Korea and China/US trade tension
The lowest fertility rate on earth
tailwinds: Trades near book value — very cheap
World leader in memory chips, riding AI demand
countries.outlook: World-class technology companies at near-book-value prices, with governance reform as the potential unlock.
countries.verdict: Cheap assets with a governance problem — if the 'value-up' reforms stick, the discount closes. That's the whole thesis, and it's a bet on culture changing.
countries.india_angle: Korea and Taiwan absorb much of the tech allocation in EM funds — the same pool of money India competes for.

countries.name: Taiwan
countries.currency_note: Stable currency, low government debt — financially well run.
risks: Cross-strait geopolitical risk — a genuine tail risk with no hedge
TSMC alone is a huge share of the index
tailwinds: The irreplaceable heart of the world's semiconductor supply chain
Enormous pricing power in advanced chips
countries.outlook: Owns the most strategically important manufacturing on earth, priced for the AI boom to continue.
countries.verdict: A wonderful business (chip-making at the frontier) with a risk you cannot diversify away or insure against. Size accordingly — this is where geopolitics, not valuation, decides the outcome.
countries.india_angle: Competes directly with India for EM tech allocations; any cross-strait scare would trigger a global risk-off that hits Nifty too.

countries.name: Hong Kong
countries.rule_of_law: Weakening — historically excellent common law, but increasingly under mainland influence
countries.currency_note: Pegged to the US dollar, so it imports US interest-rate policy whether or not that suits its economy.
risks: Effectively a leveraged bet on China's fortunes
Erosion of legal and institutional independence
tailwinds: Among the cheapest major markets in the world
The listing venue for China's best-known companies
headwinds: Dollar peg forces tight money at the wrong times
countries.outlook: Deep-value pricing on China's biggest names, with the institutional advantages that once justified a premium now fading.
countries.verdict: Statistically the cheapest thing on this map. The question isn't the price — it's whether the rules stay the same for shareholders.
countries.india_angle: Cheap China/HK versus expensive India is one of the most common rotation trades in global EM portfolios.

countries.name: Indonesia
countries.rule_of_law: Moderate — improving, with resource-nationalism policy risk
countries.currency_note: The rupiah has a long history of depreciation and crisis-time collapses — the 1998 memory is why foreign investors demand a discount.
risks: Currency vulnerability in global risk-off episodes
tailwinds: Demographics nearly as good as India's
Central to the EV battery supply chain via nickel
countries.outlook: The closest thing to 'India ten years ago' — young, growing, resource-rich, and considerably cheaper.
countries.verdict: The strongest value-plus-growth combination in Asia if you can tolerate the currency. Munger's test would be the quality of the banks and whether the state respects contracts.
countries.india_angle: The main 'other India' in EM portfolios — when India looks expensive, this is where the money often goes.

countries.name: Vietnam
countries.rule_of_law: Weak-to-moderate — one-party state, opaque, but pro-business in practice
countries.currency_note: The dong is managed and steadily devalued — a persistent, predictable drag on foreign returns.
countries.access: Hard — frontier-market status; limited fund options and foreign-ownership caps.
tailwinds: The single biggest winner from 'China+1' factory relocation
countries.outlook: The fastest-growing manufacturing story in Asia, in a market that is still hard for outsiders to own properly.
countries.verdict: Great macro story, weak shareholder infrastructure. The growth is real; the ability to actually capture it as a minority foreign holder is the open question.
countries.india_angle: India's most direct competitor for 'China+1' factory investment.

countries.name: Saudi Arabia
countries.rule_of_law: Weak by Western standards — absolute monarchy; property rights depend on the state's goodwill
countries.currency_note: Pegged to the US dollar — so for an Indian investor it behaves like dollar exposure.
countries.access: Via EM/Gulf funds; direct access is limited.
risks: Fortunes rise and fall with the oil price
Reform plans depend on oil revenue
tailwinds: Enormous sovereign wealth funding Vision 2030 diversification
countries.outlook: An oil-funded national transformation project you can buy shares in — with all the concentration and governance caveats that implies.
countries.verdict: You're underwriting one commodity and one royal family's plan. Interesting, but it fails the 'do I understand and trust the rules?' test for most investors.
countries.india_angle: Gulf oil policy sets crude prices — the single biggest external lever on Indian inflation, the rupee, and OMC/paint/aviation stocks.

countries.name: South Africa
countries.rule_of_law: Moderate — strong courts and a genuinely independent central bank, weak state capacity
countries.demographics: Young, but with very high unemployment
countries.currency_note: The rand is one of the world's most volatile currencies and a chronic depreciator — historically the single biggest destroyer of foreign investors' returns here.
risks: Chronic electricity shortages constraining the whole economy
countries.outlook: Deep-value pricing on a market with excellent mining assets bolted to a struggling domestic economy.
countries.verdict: Good businesses, difficult country. The rand means your local gains can vanish in rupee terms — a lesson in why currency IS part of the investment.
countries.india_angle: A heavy gold and platinum producer — it moves with the same safe-haven demand Indian gold investors track.

countries.name: Australia
countries.currency_note: The Aussie dollar is effectively a proxy for Chinese demand — it falls when China slows, adding to losses at the worst moment.
risks: Iron-ore revenue depends almost entirely on China
Extremely stretched housing market and household debt
Banks + miners are most of the index
countries.outlook: A high-yield miners-and-banks market that is, in practice, the cleanest listed proxy for Chinese raw-material demand.
countries.verdict: Well-run country, income-friendly market, but only two real bets: Chinese iron ore and Australian mortgages. Know that before you buy the 'diversification'.
countries.india_angle: Australian iron ore and coking coal prices feed directly into Indian steelmakers' input costs.

rotation.why: Euro-zone debt crisis. Gold hit then-record highs (~$1,900) as investors fled anything risky.
The 'taper tantrum' — the Fed hinted it would slow stimulus. Money rushed home to the US; the rupee crashed and gold fell hard.
A strong-dollar US bull market. Oil collapsed from $100 to under $30, commodity exporters suffered, gold drifted lower.
Synchronised global growth — the rare year everything worked. Money spread out into EM and cyclicals; India rallied hard.
The Fed hiked four times and the US–China trade war began. Risk assets sold off; investors hid in cash and the dollar.
The Fed pivoted to cutting rates. Both stocks AND gold rose — falling rates lift gold by making cash less rewarding to hold.
COVID crash, then a flood of central-bank money. A barbell year: money piled into US tech AND gold (a record ~$2,075).
Reopening and reflation. Money chased value, commodities and speculative assets; gold went sideways all year.
The worst inflation in 40 years and the fastest Fed hikes in decades. Almost everything fell except the dollar and energy.
The AI boom. Leadership narrowed to a handful of US giants, while gold quietly climbed on rate-cut hopes.
Rate cuts began and central banks bought gold in record size. Gold hit fresh highs alongside US tech — a risk-and-safety barbell.
Record gold on central-bank buying and de-dollarisation, plus early signs of money broadening out toward cheaper markets away from crowded US tech.

current.summary: Money is split between crowded, expensive US tech and record-high gold — investors want growth but are hedging their bets. The thing to watch is whether it broadens toward cheaper markets.
